legalStandard.name: Lack of criminal responsibility — the McHoul standard
legalStandard.test: A person is not responsible for criminal conduct if at the time of such conduct, as a result of mental disease or defect, they lack substantial capacity either to appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct or to conform their conduct to the requirements of law. The two prongs are alternatives — either one suffices.
legalStandard.burden: The Commonwealth must prove the defendant WAS criminally responsible, beyond a reasonable doubt. The defense does not have to prove insanity.
legalStandard.burdenNote: Under Commonwealth v. Lawson (2016), the mere fact that most people are sane is not, by itself, enough to carry that burden once mental-illness evidence is in the case — the Commonwealth may rely on the circumstances of the offense and the defendant's words and conduct before, during, and after.

qa.q: Does “she knew what she was doing” end the inquiry?
qa.a: No. The test has two independent prongs. Even a defendant who appreciated wrongfulness is not responsible if disease left her without substantial capacity to conform her conduct to the law. That is the prong defense expert Dr. Zeizel invoked.

qa.q: If the jury acquits on lack of criminal responsibility, does she walk free?
qa.a: No. Under M.G.L. c.123 §16, the court may order up to 40 days of hospitalization for evaluation, and the DA or facility may petition for commitment — six months initially, renewable in one-year periods. The model instruction notes a person who remains mentally ill and dangerous “may remain committed for the duration of his [or her] life.”

qa.q: What are the jury's options here?
qa.a: First-degree murder (life without parole), second-degree murder (life with parole eligibility), not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, or no unanimous verdict (mistrial; retrial possible). Whether involuntary manslaughter joins the slip is still being argued.

plainSummary: She doesn't deny causing her three children's deaths. The whole trial is one question: was her mind gone — wrecked by postpartum psychosis, as her defense says — or working fine, as prosecutors say? The experts flatly contradict each other, and a verdict could land within days.
statusNow: Closing arguments were delivered Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague argued Lindsay Clancy understood right from wrong and planned the killings; defense attorney Kevin Reddington argued she was gripped by postpartum psychosis and not criminally responsible, and had been failed by inadequate psychiatric care. Judge William Sullivan gave the case to the jury of nine women and three men, which began deliberating that afternoon and resumed Friday, Aug. 28. It must decide between not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility and guilty of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children — a conviction that carries life in prison without parole.
storySoFar: Over three weeks, about 70 prosecution witnesses built the case that Lindsay Clancy planned her children's deaths — the phone searches, the Apple Health data, the exercise bands. Then 10 defense witnesses told the opposite story: a mother 'begging for help' through months of failed treatment and 13 prescribed medications, until — two defense experts say — a psychotic break with a voice commanding her. The experts flatly contradict each other. That collision is what the jury has to resolve.
